extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians, journal editors, librarians, and academic authors interested in publishing practice and reform
extracted.subtask_description: Opinionated guidance and practical prescriptions about contributing to/organizing special issues, how authors and editors should behave, and consumer-side boycott tactics to push journals toward open access. Also brief advice for working on conjectures (collaboration, optimism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Actively look for collaborators
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek collaborators who have skills, tools, or abilities you are missing and who may have a different POV on the validity of the conjecture and how to attack it. Argue with them and learn from them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be brave and optimistic about conjectures
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether you decide to prove, disprove a conjecture, or simply state a new conjecture, go for it; ignore discouraging judgments and proceed boldly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors-in-chief should refuse special issues
rubrics_metrics.description: STOP publishing special issues! If you are an Editor in Chief, just refuse!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that special issues are often used to fill publisher page quotas, may lower standards, and enable 'blame shifting' away from the journal. Editors are responsible for journal reputation and peer review and should therefore decline guest special-issue proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors must take responsibility for peer review and reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal editors are the only ones responsible for journal reputation and for the peer review!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when guest editors are proposed, the editorial board/Editor-in-Chief should ensure oversight and be accountable for the quality of published papers; shrugging responsibility onto guest editors is unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: If organizing an honor/meeting volume, prefer a special book rather than a journal special issue
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are a potential guest editor who really wants to organize a special issue based on your conference, or to honor somebody, ask publishers to make a special book deal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special books/chapter collections avoid the perverse incentives of journal page quotas and are an appropriate home for memorials, surveys, and reminiscences that don't fit standard peer-reviewed research-issue norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author contribution quality categories for special issues (Grade A/B/C/D/F)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of typical author motivations and paper quality in special issues: A: best papers sent as homage; B: surveys or memoir-style contributions; C: name-driven/irrelevant papers; D/F: problematic or CV-padding papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grade A: authors send their best work (could've been in a better journal) — 'Grade A'. Grade B: surveys or personal reminiscences appropriate to the issue — 'Grade B'. Grade C: famous authors submit unrelated or low-effort papers relying on name recognition — 'Grade C'. Grade D/F: authors submit problematic papers to get lines on CVs or to publish work rejected elsewhere — 'Grade D/F'. The implication: authors should aim for A/B-type contributions and avoid C/D/F behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boycott all non-free journals as a consumer
rubrics_metrics.description: Boycott all non-free journals as a consumer! Do NOT download papers from journal websites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The recommended strategy is a consumer-side boycott: stop using journal websites to download articles so libraries and publishers lose leverage. This is distinct from asking people to stop refereeing/submitting; the author explicitly discourages worker-side boycotts but urges consumer-side non-use to force price negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make every paper you ever wrote freely accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: On your side as an author, make every(!) paper you ever wrote freely accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post all papers to arXiv, viXra, your own website, or anywhere search engines can find them. The author cites examples of mathematicians who do this and urges everyone to post immediately and universally to reduce reliance on paid journal access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer free versions (arXiv/author site) when accessing papers
rubrics_metrics.description: When reading papers, google it first. Google Scholar usually gives multiple download options; choose arXiv or the author's website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid MathSciNet/journal website direct downloads when a free version exists. If necessary use alternative search engines (Yandex, DuckDuckGo) to find author-posted copies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Email authors to request inaccessible papers before resorting to library/journal access
rubrics_metrics.description: If the paper is inaccessible for free, email the authors and request the file of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Politely ask authors for copies and encourage them to post papers online. The author recommends shaming non-responsive authors into posting when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: If you must use library/journal access, post the paper online afterwards
rubrics_metrics.description: If the only accessible copy is on the journal website and authors don't respond, download via your library but then post the paper online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author acknowledges this may violate copyright but argues for reposting to benefit the community and to reduce future dependence on paid access — 'be a mensch' and make the paper freely available.

rubrics_metrics.name: On course pages, link to or repost free versions for students
rubrics_metrics.description: When creating a course website, make sure all or at least most of your links are to free versions of the articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Download free copies and repost them on course sites so students do not have to go through library redirects; every link to a free copy helps reduce publisher leverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use public shaming as a lever to push authors/journals to provide free access
rubrics_metrics.description: Shaming is powerful: shame every working mathematician into posting all their papers online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues public shaming has historically worked in mathematics to correct behavior (e.g., filling gaps, acknowledging priority) and can be applied to pressure authors and journals to make work freely available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Librarians should use download metrics to gain leverage in negotiations
rubrics_metrics.description: If download data shows rapidly decreasing usage, librarians gain strong leverage to cancel or renegotiate subscriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author describes a strategy where reduced downloads of paid journal websites will convince librarians to cut subscriptions or demand lower prices; faculty posting all papers freely accelerates this effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: AMS (or large society publishers) should divest publishing or create a Chinese wall
rubrics_metrics.description: The AMS should sell its journal business to some university press and invest long-term the sale profits, or create a 'Chinese wall' separating publishing from other AMS activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This advice is aimed at resolving conflicts of interest where professional societies both lobby for open access and profit from journal publishing; divestment or separation would remove incentives against free publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't boycott by refusing to submit or referee (work-side boycott)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do NOT boycott anyone specifically by refusing to submit or referee for leading journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author believes worker-side boycotts are impractical and counterproductive; instead, change should come from consumer behavior and systemic measures rather than asking individuals to give up submitting/refereeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use search-first workflow to avoid journal website clicks (MathSciNet/web-search suggestion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid clicking through to publisher websites from services like MathSciNet; search for free copies first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author suggests adding a 'web search' button to MathSciNet that would search Google Scholar or similar to help users find free versions and reduce unnecessary publisher site visits.
